parts.label: (a)
parts.text: With reference to the direction of transfer of energy, compare the oscillations of transverse and longitudinal progressive waves.

markscheme_points.text: longitudinal waves have oscillations parallel to the (direction of) transfer of energy
transverse waves have oscillations perpendicular to the (direction of) transfer of energy

hints: Hint 1: Think of a wave as carrying energy from one place to another. Now ask yourself - in which direction do the individual particles vibrate compared to that energy journey?
Hint 2: Picture a rope shaken up and down versus a slinky pushed back and forth. Which one vibrates across the energy path and which one vibrates along it?
parts.proper_answer: In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of transfer of energy. In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to the direction of transfer of energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What defines the two wave types**
Think of energy moving from the source outward. The particles of the medium oscillate around a fixed mean position, but the direction of that oscillation is what matters. Transverse means across, longitudinal means along.

Step 2: **State both comparisons clearly**
For transverse, e.g. light or a rope wave: particles move up-down while energy moves left-right, so $$\text{oscillation} \perp \text{energy transfer}$$. For longitudinal, e.g. sound: particles compress and rarefy back and forth in the same line as the energy moves, so $$\text{oscillation} \parallel \text{energy transfer}$$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 4.1, draw a letter A at the position of an antinode.

markscheme_points.text: A marked at the open end of the pipe

hints: Hint 1: Recall where air can move most freely in this pipe - at the closed piston or at the open end - and what maximum vibration means for a stationary sound wave.
parts.proper_answer: Letter A marked at the open end of the pipe (position of maximum displacement amplitude).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Antinode means maximum movement**
In a stationary sound wave, a node N is where air molecules hardly move, and an antinode A is where they oscillate with maximum amplitude. Look at Fig. 4.1 - the envelope is widest at the right-hand side.

Step 2: **Apply the pipe end rules**
At the closed piston air cannot move, so there must be a displacement node. At the open end air can move freely in and out, so there must be a displacement antinode. So you mark A at the open end on the right.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Determine the frequency of the sound wave.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 4.1 and count fractions of a wavelength - how much of a full sine wave fits between the node at the piston and the antinode at the open end?
Hint 2: Use the given pipe length of $4.5 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$ to work out the full wavelength $\lambda$ from that fraction.
Hint 3: Link wavelength to frequency using the speed of sound - which form of $v = f\lambda$ will give you $f$?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the wavelength from the pipe length**
You have a node at the closed piston and an antinode at the open end. That node to antinode distance is one quarter of a wavelength, $\lambda/4$. So: $$\frac{\lambda}{4} = 4.5 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$$ $$\lambda = 4 \times 4.5 \times 10^{-2} = 0.18\text{ m}$$

Step 2: **Use the wave equation to get frequency**
Sound speed is fixed by the air: $$v = f\lambda$$ Rearrange before substituting: $$f = \frac{v}{\lambda}$$ $$f = \frac{340}{0.18} \approx 1889\text{ Hz} \approx 1900\text{ Hz}$$ Give 2 s.f. to match the data.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The piston is moved to the left. The frequency of the sound wave emitted by the loudspeaker is then changed so that a stationary wave is formed with same number of antinodes as in Fig. 4.1.

State and explain the change that is made to the frequency of the sound wave.

markscheme_points.text: the node–antinode distance is longer or the wavelength (of the wave) is longer
(the speed of sound is constant so) the frequency (of the wave) is lower

hints: Hint 1: If the piston moves left but you still keep only one node and one antinode, what must happen to the physical length of that quarter-wave pattern?
Hint 2: With speed of sound $v$ unchanged in the same air, how must frequency respond if wavelength gets longer to still satisfy $v = f\lambda$?
parts.proper_answer: The frequency is decreased. The longer pipe length means the node-antinode distance and hence wavelength is longer, and since $v = f\lambda$ with $v$ constant, $f$ must be lower.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Longer pipe means longer wavelength**
Moving the piston left increases the resonant length $L$. You still have the same pattern, $L = \lambda/4$, so $\lambda = 4L$ must increase. The node-antinode distance is stretched.

Step 2: **Frequency must fall to keep v constant**
Speed of sound in air stays at $340\text{ m s}^{-1}$. From $$v = f\lambda$$, $f$ and $\lambda$ are inversely proportional: $$f = v/\lambda$$ A larger $\lambda$ gives a smaller $f$. So you lower the loudspeaker frequency to restore resonance.

key_concepts: inverse relation of f and lambda at constant v
